idiom_name: one function per rule over a token stream + shared peek/expect helpers
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the token stream and a cursor in one parser state object, write one function per grammar rule (its body is the rule's right-hand side - terminals consume tokens, nonterminals call their functions, alternatives are branches, repetition is a loop, optionals are conditionals), and route every consumption through shared helpers that report positioned errors. Rewrite left recursion into iteration before writing any code, and choose the error strategy per rule (abort, synchronise, or insert a missing token). Keep the recursion depth bounded and one parser instance per input; the grammar must stay visible next to the functions that implement it.
code_sketch:
parse(input):
    toks = lex(input)                      # tokens with positions
    return ruleStart(toks, 0)              # one function per grammar rule

ruleA(state):
    left = ruleB(state)                    # nonterminal -> call
    while state.peek().kind in followSet:  # repetition -> loop
        state.next()
        left = node(left, ruleB(state))
    return left                            # alternatives -> branch on lookahead
pitfalls: Skipping the left-recursion rewrite and relying on a depth guard to stop the runaway recursion, which converts a grammar bug into a truncated parse.
Sharing parser state (cursor, diagnostics, depth) across parses or threads, so results depend on the previous input.
Letting rules do more than parse (resolving names, computing types, performing I/O), which destroys single-pass testability and couples passes that should stay separate.

Wrong move: use recursive calls with no nesting or token budget on untrusted input -> deeply nested input can exhaust the host stack before a parse error is reported -> instead enforce explicit depth/input limits and fail at the token position.

Wrong move: dispatch alternatives by speculative parse-and-rollback when FIRST sets overlap -> repeated retries can make malformed input superlinear or exponential and degrade diagnostics -> instead left-factor the grammar and use bounded lookahead, reserving backtracking for measured cases.

Wrong move: treat precedence as a ladder of recursive rules copied from a left-recursive grammar -> associativity and precedence drift as operators are added -> instead use a loop, precedence-climbing routine or Pratt layer for expression subgrammars.
